claims.text: The combination of high configurational entropy and a high density of nanoscale grain boundaries causes sluggish atomic diffusion in high-entropy nanoalloys.
Sluggish diffusion kinetically suppresses phase separation at high temperatures.
Sluggish diffusion kinetically suppresses chemical segregation at high temperatures.
The proposed initial material is a single-phase, potentially BCC, nanoalloy with homogeneous elemental distribution.
Nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloys can exhibit high thermal stability.
Nanoscale grain boundaries provide energy barriers to atomic motion.
The high density of nanoscale grain boundaries contributes to sluggish diffusion.
High configurational entropy minimizes the thermodynamic driving force for elemental segregation.
The combined thermodynamic and kinetic effects prevent secondary-phase formation and elemental clustering at elevated temperatures.
The nanoalloy will retain its single-phase structure during the specified high-temperature treatment.
The nanoalloy will undergo less elemental segregation than a coarse-grained sample of the same composition.
The nanoalloy will undergo less microstructural change than a coarse-grained sample of the same composition.
A coarse-grained version of the same alloy will exhibit faster diffusion-driven phase separation or elemental segregation.
Refractory high-entropy alloys are relevant to high-temperature aerospace, reactor, and other extreme-environment applications.
Above an unspecified threshold, thermodynamic forces can overcome the proposed kinetic barriers.
Failure of the nanoalloy to show a significantly slower rate of phase change or segregation than the coarse-grained control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The treatment is specified to occur before the onset of thermodynamically driven phase transitions, yet phase separation or phase change under that same treatment is an expected baseline behavior and a principal measured outcome.
